chapter: Telephone reels: blues and Bessie Smith
title: What attracted him to the blues and what the blues is
summary: He grew up in the era, defines the blues as a mountain, and calls it a living tradition.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the blues is, and why every jazz player needs it

blocks.x: The name of the game, so to speak. So let me see. I had a couple of questions to ask you. (Inaudible) because I got so interested in these blues reference books and blues books. What attracted you to the blues?

Well, just all the time there was -- I grew up through that era. And growing up that way, why I heard so much of it and just, why you learn to like some part of it. Some parts you don't. So this is (inaudible).
It was --
I came way back from ragtime, you know. So that's one of those things.
Yeah, how -- what would your definition of the blues be, J. C.?
Oh, that's difficult to say. My definition of the blues, that's nearly a mountain.
True.
You ask someone else and see if they know and don't say it's a mountain too.
That's excellent. I did read someplace somebody called it "the dark underside of jazz."

HEMLOCK
MR. JOHNSON: Yeah, that's very nice.

Isn't that good? You know -- do you know what I felt good about? When I was reading about it, it said that the blues to some people is like folklore, that it's part of an era gone, and then others say that it's a living tradition. And which do you feel it is?
It's a living tradition.

I knew you were going to say that. And you know what? Remember when I was apologizing to you, when I said that I still feel blues, you know, permeating music in society, and I was talking about country-western, and then I apologized to you?
Sure.
But, you know, I read somewhere that the blues was a shaping influence, you know, on American music from jazz to country and western to rock and roll. There's that blues influence.
Yeah.
And you realize, of course, it's there, even though it's -- the base is the blues, as you know it.
Yeah, it's there. They don't use it as much now as they used to.
Right.
But it crept in there. It got in the veins.
veins.
